transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… mostly because work’s been getting messy. I’m an electrician, and lately I can’t stay on one estimate or code form long enough to finish it. Like, I’ll be trying to write up one job, then a tool drops or my phone buzzes, or I’ll suddenly think of some better setup for the workshop, and I’m gone. Then I come back and I’ve mixed up details between jobs.

It sounds small when I say it, but it’s been happening enough that I figured I should probably talk to somebody.
Did you have this kind of trouble focusing when you were a child?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I remember school being… school. I wasn’t the kid who loved sitting still for math or anything, but I don’t know if that was a “focus problem” or just being a kid. I did better in classes where I could use my hands—shop class, fixing stuff, that kind of thing.

My mom would probably remember better. She keeps all this old school paperwork in a box somewhere, like report cards and random certificates, even one from a science fair where I made this terrible little motor thing that barely worked. But as far as whether it was like what’s happening now… I don’t know. I can’t really say.
Have there been times when you felt unusually energized and needed much less sleep than usual?

Yeah… yeah, that’s been happening. For, I don’t know, months now I’ll sleep maybe three or four hours and then I’m just up before dawn like my brain’s already clocked in. I’ll start pricing materials or answering emails, or I’ll sketch out some wiring setup or system idea like it’s totally normal to be doing that at 4:30 in the morning.

And the weird part is I don’t always feel wrecked from it. Like if I only slept that much after a long job, normally I’d be useless, but lately I’ll pop up feeling like I got a full night, at least at first. Then I get into the day and there’s all this stuff I’m trying to do, and—sorry, I’m getting off track—but yeah, much less sleep and still feeling pretty energized.
During these times when you sleep only three or four hours, do you also feel unusually cheerful or high compared with your normal self?

Yeah, I guess “cheerful” is part of it, but it’s more like… pumped up. Like I’ll be talking a mile a minute about how our little shop could become the main solar outfit in town, like it’s obviously going to happen if everyone just gets on board.

And then if my wife is like, “Maybe slow down,” or one of the apprentices asks some normal question about the plan, I can snap at them. Not screaming or anything, but sharp—like they’re being stupid for not seeing it. Which, later, I know is not really fair.
During those pumped-up times, do you do things that are unusually risky or impulsive for you?

I’m not sure what counts as risky, exactly. Like, I don’t think I’m out doing wild stuff just for the thrill of it or anything.

I mean, I’ll make decisions faster than usual, maybe jump into ideas before I’ve really thought them through, but then again that’s kind of how work is sometimes—you’ve got a problem in front of you and you just have to solve it. Like last week we had this panel situation where the layout was all wrong, and I got thinking about how the supplier really should’ve caught that, because if they had just labeled the boxes better—

Sorry. What do you mean by risky? Like spending money, driving fast, that kind of thing? I haven’t really thought about it that way.
Have there been times when you felt unusually irritable compared with your normal self?

Yeah… irritable is probably the right word. It’s like I’ll be in this big, fired-up mood, talking about how our shop is about to take over solar work around here, and it all feels so obvious to me.

But then if my wife says something like, “Is that realistic?” or one of the apprentices asks a basic question about the plan, I can just flip kind of fast. Not, like, throwing things, but I get sharp with them, like they’re slowing me down or not getting it. And then later I’m thinking, why did I react like that? It wasn’t even a big deal.
During those fired-up times, do you feel more confident or capable than usual?

Yeah… I do. I mean, in the moment it feels less like “confidence” and more like, why wouldn’t I be able to do this?

Like I’ll start thinking I can take on these bigger commercial jobs, train up a whole crew, have everyone running under me, basically build the shop into something way bigger right now. And I know, if I’m being honest, there are parts of that where my licensing and experience aren’t totally where they’d need to be yet.

But when I’m in that fired-up mode, that little practical part just gets kind of… quiet. It feels like I can figure it out as I go.
Have these fired-up periods caused serious problems at work or at home?

Yeah… I mean, I wouldn’t have called it “serious” at first, because work is always messy, you know? Scheduling is a nightmare anyway, especially when one job runs long and then the supplier drops stuff at the wrong site, and then everyone acts like it’s your fault—

But, yeah. Clients have started complaining. Like I missed details I usually wouldn’t miss, or I’ll have two things lined up in a way that doesn’t really make sense, scheduling-wise. And my apprentices… I can tell they don’t really trust my direction the same way. They double-check me more, or they hesitate.

At home it’s worse, honestly. My wife and I keep circling the same arguments about the mortgage and the business. She feels like I’m putting everything we’ve built at risk, and I get why she says it, even if in the moment I don’t want to hear it.
When you get into one of these fired-up periods, does it last at least a week?

Yeah… I mean, it’s hard to slice it up neatly into, like, “this week” and “that week.” It feels more like it’s been building for months.

Probably since we took on the mortgage for the workshop and bought the equipment — so, what, about seven months now? That’s when everything started feeling more intense, like I had to keep pushing, keep proving the shop could handle it. I know that’s not exactly what you asked, but it hasn’t just been a day or two thing.
During these fired-up periods, have you ever heard or seen things that other people said weren’t there, or believed something others thought was clearly untrue?

I don’t think so… not like seeing people who aren’t there or hearing voices, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, I’ll get really locked onto an idea and other people will act like I’m being ridiculous, but it feels more like they’re not seeing the whole picture yet. Like with the shop, my wife will say, “That’s not realistic,” and then we end up arguing about numbers and timing and whether the suppliers can actually keep up — and half the time the suppliers are the real problem anyway, because they’ll tell you one thing on the phone and then the order shows up missing parts—

Sorry. No, I don’t think I’ve had, like, hallucinations or anything. Believing stuff… I guess people think I’m overestimating what I can pull off, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean by clearly untrue.
During one of these fired-up periods, have you ever needed to go to the hospital because of how you were acting or feeling?

No, not to the hospital. I mean, there have been times people made it sound like I was acting… I don’t know, out of control or not listening, but nobody’s taken me to the ER or anything like that.

My wife did say once I needed to “get help,” but that was in the middle of an argument, and we were already stressed about the shop and the bills and— yeah, no, I haven’t been hospitalized for it.
During those fired-up times, do your thoughts race so fast that it’s hard to keep up with them?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, sometimes I’ve got a lot on my mind, sure — work stuff, money stuff, scheduling, whether a job’s going to get delayed because somebody didn’t order the right breaker or the permit office is dragging their feet…

But “racing” like I can’t keep up with them? I don’t know. Maybe it feels busy in my head, but I’ve also always had a lot to juggle. My wife says I jump from one thing to another when I’m talking, but that’s different, right? Or maybe that’s what you mean. I’m not totally sure.
Between these fired-up periods, do you return to your usual self?

I guess… mostly? I mean, that’s hard to pin down because what’s “usual,” you know? Like my wife would probably say I’m never completely easy to live with, but I think I settle back into just doing work, coming home, dealing with the normal stuff.

It’s not like I’m keeping track on a calendar or anything. Sometimes after a stretch like that I’m tired or things are messy because I’ve taken on too much, and then you’re dealing with the fallout, which can look like you’re still not yourself. Like if a job runs over budget, you don’t just wake up the next week and everything’s fixed.

But yeah… I think I go back to more or less normal. I don’t know exactly how to answer it better than that.
When you’re in one of these fired-up periods, do you take on a lot more projects or work than you normally would?

Yeah… I mean, yes, probably. When I’m like that I’ll say yes to way more than I normally should. I’ll go from a job site straight to looking at a bid, then back to the workshop messing with test panels or wiring something up, and then I’ll get some idea about home automation—like, “Oh, this would be easy, I can build that”—even though the last thing isn’t finished yet.

It doesn’t feel like too much at the time. It feels like sitting still is just… wasting time, you know? Like there’s momentum and I don’t want to lose it. Then later it’s like, okay, why did I start three different things when one would’ve been enough.
During those fired-up periods, do you get much more done or start a lot more purposeful work than usual?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, I’ll get on a roll and it’s like I can’t just do the one thing. I’ll go from job sites to checking out new bids, then end up in the workshop rewiring some test panel or messing with some setup that probably could’ve waited.

And then I’ll get this idea for some home-automation thing — like lights or sensors or whatever — and I’m starting that before I’ve even finished the last project. At the time it feels productive, like I’m using the energy right. Sitting still feels like wasting time. Then later I look around and it’s like… okay, I started a lot. Maybe too much.
During those fired-up periods, do you talk much more than usual or feel hard to stop once you get going?

I don’t know… maybe? I mean, I talk a lot anyway, depending who you ask. My wife would probably roll her eyes at that.

When I’m working, especially on a job, you kind of have to talk through things — like if you’re explaining to an apprentice why something’s wired wrong, or trying to get a contractor to understand why their timeline makes no sense. And some people just don’t listen the first time, so then you end up saying it three different ways.

But hard to stop… I’m not sure I notice it like that. I guess once I get into explaining something I can keep going, but I don’t know if that’s one of those periods or just me being me.
During those fired-up periods, have you spent much more money than usual?

I don’t know if it’s much more. I mean, I’ll buy stuff for projects sometimes — parts, tools, little smart switches or sensors, whatever — but with electrical work there’s always some reason you can justify buying a thing, you know?

Like, if I’m at the supply house, it’s easy to be like, “Well, I’ll use that eventually,” and then you get home and realize you already had one in a bin somewhere. I’ve got bins of parts that… honestly I should probably label better, because then I wouldn’t be buying duplicates.

But as far as like, going crazy with money or something, I don’t know. I haven’t really tracked it that closely. My wife might have a better answer than me.
During these fired-up periods, does it get so severe that you can’t function normally at work or at home?

Yeah… I mean, “can’t function” sounds kind of dramatic, but it’s definitely been affecting things.

At work, I’ll think I’ve got everything handled, and then a client’s like, “You said you were coming Tuesday,” or there’s some detail I missed that I normally wouldn’t. And that’s embarrassing, because I’ve built a lot on being the guy who catches that stuff. Even my apprentices… I can tell they don’t trust my direction the same way sometimes, like they’re double-checking me more.

And at home it’s… yeah, it’s a problem. My wife and I keep getting into it about the mortgage, the business, all of that. She thinks I’m risking what we’ve built, and I get why she says it, even if in the moment I feel like I’m just trying to keep things moving.
During these fired-up times, have you ever been completely certain of something that other people said was impossible or clearly untrue?

Completely certain? I don’t know if I’d say impossible, exactly. It’s more like… during those times I get this feeling like I could take on bigger commercial jobs, like right now, and build out a whole crew and train them up.

And I mean, part of that isn’t crazy — I know the work, I’ve been doing electrical a long time, and half the problem in this trade is people not being taught right in the first place. I had this one guy years ago who showed me a panel layout that was just… anyway, that kind of thing makes me think I could do it better.

But then if I’m being honest, part of me knows my licensing and experience aren’t quite where they’d need to be for all of that. My wife will point that out, or someone will say, “You’re not set up for that yet,” and in the moment I’m like, no, you just don’t see it. So… yeah, I guess I get pretty convinced I can do more than maybe I actually can right then.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, sometimes I’ve got a lot on my mind, sure — work stuff, money stuff, scheduling, whether a job’s going to get delayed because somebody didn’t order the right breaker or the permit office is dragging their feet…

But “racing” like I can’t keep up with them? I don’t know. Maybe it feels busy in my head, but I’ve also always had a lot to juggle. My wife says I jump from one thing to another when I’m talking, but that’s different, right? Or maybe that’s what you mean. I’m not totally sure.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the elevated/irritable energized state is episodic with a distinct return to baseline, which helps distinguish bipolar disorder from chronic ADHD or stress-related symptoms.
doctor.question: Between these fired-up periods, do you return to your usual self?

target_item.reason: The question asks about returning to baseline between fired-up periods, but the provided symptom profile does not include an item about inter-episode recovery or baseline functioning.

patient.answer:
I guess… mostly? I mean, that’s hard to pin down because what’s “usual,” you know? Like my wife would probably say I’m never completely easy to live with, but I think I settle back into just doing work, coming home, dealing with the normal stuff.

It’s not like I’m keeping track on a calendar or anything. Sometimes after a stretch like that I’m tired or things are messy because I’ve taken on too much, and then you’re dealing with the fallout, which can look like you’re still not yourself. Like if a job runs over budget, you don’t just wake up the next week and everything’s fixed.

But yeah… I think I go back to more or less normal. I don’t know exactly how to answer it better than that.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the fired-up episodes include increased goal-directed activity, which would help distinguish bipolar mania/hypomania from ADHD, anxiety, stress reactions, or depression.
doctor.question: When you’re in one of these fired-up periods, do you take on a lot more projects or work than you normally would?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been going nonstop from job sites to bids to rewiring test panels in the workshop, starting new home-automation ideas before the last one is done because sitting still feels like wasting time.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during fired-up periods, I take on substantially more work or projects than usual, which directly reflects increased goal-directed activity and energy.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, yes, probably. When I’m like that I’ll say yes to way more than I normally should. I’ll go from a job site straight to looking at a bid, then back to the workshop messing with test panels or wiring something up, and then I’ll get some idea about home automation—like, “Oh, this would be easy, I can build that”—even though the last thing isn’t finished yet.

It doesn’t feel like too much at the time. It feels like sitting still is just… wasting time, you know? Like there’s momentum and I don’t want to lose it. Then later it’s like, okay, why did I start three different things when one would’ve been enough.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated episodes include increased goal-directed activity, a core manic symptom that helps confirm bipolar disorder over ADHD, anxiety, adjustment disorder, or depression.
doctor.question: During those fired-up periods, do you get much more done or start a lot more purposeful work than usual?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been going nonstop from job sites to bids to rewiring test panels in the workshop, starting new home-automation ideas before the last one is done because sitting still feels like wasting time.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about increased goal-directed activity during fired-up periods, specifically getting more done or starting more purposeful work than usual.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. I mean, I’ll get on a roll and it’s like I can’t just do the one thing. I’ll go from job sites to checking out new bids, then end up in the workshop rewiring some test panel or messing with some setup that probably could’ve waited.

And then I’ll get this idea for some home-automation thing — like lights or sensors or whatever — and I’m starting that before I’ve even finished the last project. At the time it feels productive, like I’m using the energy right. Sitting still feels like wasting time. Then later I look around and it’s like… okay, I started a lot. Maybe too much.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fired-up periods included increased talkativeness/pressured speech, a key manic symptom that would further distinguish bipolar disorder from ADHD, anxiety, depression, or stress-related causes.
doctor.question: During those fired-up periods, do you talk much more than usual or feel hard to stop once you get going?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about being more talkative or feeling hard to stop talking during fired-up periods, which corresponds to pressured speech. That symptom is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… maybe? I mean, I talk a lot anyway, depending who you ask. My wife would probably roll her eyes at that.

When I’m working, especially on a job, you kind of have to talk through things — like if you’re explaining to an apprentice why something’s wired wrong, or trying to get a contractor to understand why their timeline makes no sense. And some people just don’t listen the first time, so then you end up saying it three different ways.

But hard to stop… I’m not sure I notice it like that. I guess once I get into explaining something I can keep going, but I don’t know if that’s one of those periods or just me being me.

inference.note: Symptoms now strongly support a manic episode without psychotic symptoms: decreased need for sleep, elevated/irritable mood, increased goal-directed activity, overconfidence/grandiosity, excessive involvement in work/projects, and impairment lasting at least a week. This narrows away from primary depressive disorder (F32.9) and makes bipolar spectrum more likely; upgraded from unspecified bipolar disorder to F31.1 as leading candidate while retaining some differentials.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether he has made unusually risky financial decisions during the fired-up periods, which helps distinguish bipolar hypomania/mania from ADHD or stress-related distractibility.
doctor.question: During those fired-up periods, have you spent much more money than usual?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about increased spending during fired-up periods, but the provided symptom profile does not include a distinct item for excessive spending or financially risky behavior.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if it’s much more. I mean, I’ll buy stuff for projects sometimes — parts, tools, little smart switches or sensors, whatever — but with electrical work there’s always some reason you can justify buying a thing, you know?

Like, if I’m at the supply house, it’s easy to be like, “Well, I’ll use that eventually,” and then you get home and realize you already had one in a bin somewhere. I’ve got bins of parts that… honestly I should probably label better, because then I wouldn’t be buying duplicates.

But as far as like, going crazy with money or something, I don’t know. I haven’t really tracked it that closely. My wife might have a better answer than me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/irritable, decreased-sleep state causes marked functional impairment, which best distinguishes bipolar I mania from hypomania/other causes.
doctor.question: During these fired-up periods, does it get so severe that you can’t function normally at work or at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: Clients have started complaining about missed details and mixed-up scheduling, and my apprentices don’t trust my direction the way they used to. At home, the mortgage and the business are turning into constant arguments because my wife feels like I’m putting everything we built at risk.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the fired-up periods become severe enough to impair normal functioning at work or home, which directly matches the functional impairment profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, “can’t function” sounds kind of dramatic, but it’s definitely been affecting things.

At work, I’ll think I’ve got everything handled, and then a client’s like, “You said you were coming Tuesday,” or there’s some detail I missed that I normally wouldn’t. And that’s embarrassing, because I’ve built a lot on being the guy who catches that stuff. Even my apprentices… I can tell they don’t trust my direction the same way sometimes, like they’re double-checking me more.

And at home it’s… yeah, it’s a problem. My wife and I keep getting into it about the mortgage, the business, all of that. She thinks I’m risking what we’ve built, and I get why she says it, even if in the moment I feel like I’m just trying to keep things moving.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the mood episodes have included unequivocal psychotic features, which would strongly separate bipolar I mania from bipolar disorder unspecified and from ADHD/anxiety/stress-related explanations.
doctor.question: During these fired-up times, have you ever been completely certain of something that other people said was impossible or clearly untrue?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I keep feeling like I can take on commercial jobs and train a whole crew right now, even though part of me knows my licensing and experience aren’t quite where they need to be for all that.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about being completely certain of beliefs others see as impossible or untrue during fired-up periods, which most directly relates to grandiosity or inflated self-esteem.

patient.answer:
Completely certain? I don’t know if I’d say impossible, exactly. It’s more like… during those times I get this feeling like I could take on bigger commercial jobs, like right now, and build out a whole crew and train them up.

And I mean, part of that isn’t crazy — I know the work, I’ve been doing electrical a long time, and half the problem in this trade is people not being taught right in the first place. I had this one guy years ago who showed me a panel layout that was just… anyway, that kind of thing makes me think I could do it better.

But then if I’m being honest, part of me knows my licensing and experience aren’t quite where they’d need to be for all of that. My wife will point that out, or someone will say, “You’re not set up for that yet,” and in the moment I’m like, no, you just don’t see it. So… yeah, I guess I get pretty convinced I can do more than maybe I actually can right then.

inference.note: Symptoms support a manic/hypomanic spectrum episode: decreased need for sleep, elevated/irritable mood, increased goal-directed activity, overconfidence/grandiosity, functional impairment lasting at least a week or more. ADHD/anxiety/trauma-related diagnoses are less explanatory for the episodic fired-up periods and decreased need for sleep, so they were dropped.

No hallucinations, delusions, or hospitalization were confirmed. This supports bipolar affective disorder, current episode manic without psychotic symptoms, rather than the unspecified bipolar code.
